solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: This is missing pocketbook for machine which screws up?

indicators.note: the clue says its own opening word lacks the two letters of the word that follows it, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written, before it loses the letters of 'is'
a reader is a book, here one small enough for the pocket

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a contraption which messes things up has lost its little notebook.
explanation.walkthrough: THIS without IS leaves TH, then READER. The question mark flags that 'screws up' means cuts screw threads, not makes a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: A threader is a tool or machine that cuts screw threads, so it literally produces the spirals on a screw.

clue.text: Bugle-call at GI's burial is piercing

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the US military bugle call played at funerals and lights-out

definitions.note: 'is piercing' stands for the verb form 'taps', i.e. pierces
definitions.meaning: second meaning: ... as a verb, making a hole in a cask or tree

explanation.surface: A bugle sounding at an American soldier's funeral cuts through the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piercing' looks like an adjective for a shrill note; it is the verb sense of tapping a barrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Taps is the American last-post call, and to tap a cask is to pierce it to draw off liquid.

clue.text: You say this on finding His Eminence outside before show

indicators.note: the abbreviation for the cardinal's title sits on the outside, wrapping round what follows it

parts.note: HE is the standard abbreviation for His Eminence, a cardinal's title
ere is an old word for before
to wear something is to display or show it

explanation.surface: A greeting to a cardinal discovered just before a performance begins.
explanation.walkthrough: His Eminence is a cardinal's title; 'outside' means its two letters wrap round the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the everyday exclamation made when you locate what you were looking for or arrive somewhere.

clue.text: City understanding what constitutes warning

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro, the Brazilian city
tact is sensitive understanding of others

explanation.surface: Urban sympathy is what makes up a caution.
explanation.walkthrough: The Riot Act was a British law read aloud to disperse crowds; 'reading the riot act' now means giving a stern telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: Reading someone the riot act is idiomatically giving them a severe reprimand or final caution.

clue.text: Birds gather moving south as far as poss

indicators.text: moving south as far as poss
indicators.note: in a down entry south is the bottom, so a letter travels all the way from the top to the foot

parts.note: to save is to gather up or collect

explanation.surface: Birds flock together and fly as far south as they can for the winter.
explanation.walkthrough: The S at the top of SAVE drops to the bottom of the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Aves is the Latin name of the zoological class containing all birds.

clue.text: Disco may pass drug test

indicators.note: a pass in football moves the ball on, and here the letters are moved around into new places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nightclub might get through a narcotics screening.
explanation.definitionFit: Docimasy is an old term for assaying, including testing drugs or metals for purity.

clue.text: Comparatively sparse portion of land fenced off by Bishop

indicators.note: something fenced off is enclosed on all sides, so the land measure is held inside the churchman

parts.note: RR is Right Reverend, the style of a bishop
an are is a metric land measure of 100 square metres

explanation.surface: A bishop has enclosed a small plot that is thinner on the ground than most.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare can mean thinly spread or sparse, so its comparative is more sparse.

clue.text: Gent is full of it and can go forth

indicators.note: a vessel that is full of something holds it inside, so the gentleman's title surrounds the pronoun

parts.note: sir is a way of addressing a gentleman
't is the clipped form of it, as in 'tis

explanation.surface: A man is so full of himself that he is free to set out.
explanation.walkthrough: S(T)IR. The answer then has two separate meanings: slang for prison, and to move out of doors.
explanation.definitionFit: Stir is slang for prison, as is can; and to stir is to move or venture out.

clue.text: Small pet cut item of tack

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a pet is a fit of sulking, like a tiff
bit is the past tense of bite, to cut with the teeth

explanation.surface: A small animal snipped through a piece of horse equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: Tack is horse-riding gear; a pet in the sense of a huff matches a tiff.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiff bit is a rigid mouthpiece for a horse's bridle, part of its tack.

clue.text: Moniker for the very tall (?) child who chases up centre-half

indicators.note: in a down entry 'up' means reading from the bottom towards the top

parts.note: in the playground game of tag the chaser is called 'it'
CH is the abbreviation for the football position centre-half

explanation.surface: A nickname for a lanky child who runs after a football defender.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed question mark signals irony: Tich, from music-hall star Little Tich, is a nickname for a small person, given to a tall one as a tease.
explanation.definitionFit: Tich is a nickname for a short person, applied ironically to someone very tall, like calling a giant Tiny.

clue.text: Prompt monarch's up above PA

indicators.note: in a down entry 'up' means the royal letters are read bottom to top

parts.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen; the 's stands for 'is'
a personal assistant can act as a minder

explanation.surface: The king is promptly put in charge of his personal assistant.
explanation.definitionFit: A reminder is a prompt: a note or cue that jogs someone's memory.

clue.text: Redolent of English case

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
the vocative is the grammatical case of address

explanation.surface: Something smells strongly of an English legal case.
explanation.definitionFit: Evocative of and redolent of both mean strongly suggestive or reminiscent of something.

clue.text: Stay for opening of Parliament

parts.note: pro is Latin for 'for', as in pros and cons

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that one is taken

parts.note: the initial letter of the word

explanation.surface: Remain behind for the state opening of Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stay' looks like a verb but is the noun: a support.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay is a support or brace, and a prop is likewise something that holds a thing up.

clue.text: Charles and one Commonwealth economic association

parts.note: Car. is a dictionary abbreviation for Carolus, Latin for Charles
I is the Roman numeral one
Com. is an abbreviation for Commonwealth

explanation.surface: King Charles and a single Commonwealth trade body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonwealth' seems part of the definition, since CARICOM's members are mostly Commonwealth states, but it supplies the last three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: CARICOM, the Caribbean Community, is a regional bloc promoting economic integration among its member states.

clue.text: Discount place pictured by McGill? Time to enter

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so the time abbreviation goes into the holiday spot

parts.note: Donald McGill drew the famous saucy British seaside postcards
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A cut-price holiday resort of the kind seen on cheeky postcards, and it is time to go in.
explanation.walkthrough: SE(T)ASIDE. 'Discount' is the verb: to disregard.
explanation.definitionFit: To discount an argument is to set it aside, dismissing it from consideration.

clue.text: Flipping pound reduced wealth and shilling stops in the past

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it the other way, so the word is read backwards
reduced means cut down, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to pound is to crush
ease as in comfort and affluence, 'living at ease'
s was the abbreviation for the old British shilling coin

explanation.surface: Bad-tempered complaint that the pound has fallen and money and the old shilling are things of the past.
explanation.walkthrough: CRUSH loses its H, then reverses. 'In the past' marks surcease as an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: Surcease is an archaic verb meaning to cease or bring to an end, so surceases means stops.

clue.text: Flourish of letter with frame circling

indicators.note: circling means going all the way round, so the frame encloses the abbreviation

parts.note: a sash is the sliding frame of a window
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: A decorative letter in a picture frame.
explanation.walkthrough: SA(W)SH. 'Letter' looks like the wordplay but belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A swash is a decorative tail or flourish on a printed character, as in swash capitals.

clue.text: Save blade on plough — accepted and established routine

parts.note: sock is an old word for a ploughshare
A is an abbreviation for accepted
a way is a habitual manner of doing things

explanation.surface: A farmer protects the ploughshare, having adopted a settled method.
explanation.definitionFit: To sock away money is an informal idiom for putting it aside as savings.

clue.text: Glass is more readily filled by Chaplain

indicators.note: something filled by another holds it inside, so the comparison word takes in the clergyman

parts.note: sooner means more willingly, as in 'I'd sooner stay'
Ch. is the abbreviation for chaplain

explanation.surface: A drinking glass is gladly topped up by the padre.
explanation.walkthrough: S(CH)OONER.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is a large glass, for sherry in Britain or beer in Australia and the US.

clue.text: War poet troubled about bit of miracle fruit in LLL

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters wrap round the single letter
troubled means disturbed, so the letters of the poet phrase are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is just its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A soldier-poet is shaken by a small wonder in a Shakespeare comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: LLL is Love's Labour's Lost, where Holofernes mentions the pomewater, an old apple variety.
explanation.definitionFit: The pomwater was a large juicy apple, the fruit named in Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost.

clue.text: Pleasure carrying about Mr Tumnus or his ilk

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so the word for enjoyment holds the abbreviation inside

parts.note: fun is enjoyment or pleasure
a. is an abbreviation for about, like circa

explanation.surface: Enjoyment surrounds the goat-legged character from Narnia and his kind.
explanation.walkthrough: F(A)UN. Mr Tumnus is the faun in C.S. Lewis's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Tumnus is an example of a faun, a woodland creature of Roman myth, half man and half goat.

clue.text: Potentially big lad or I should be shut up

indicators.note: potentially means what something could become, so the letters may become a different word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hefty young man, or I myself, could end up locked away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' reads as a joining word, but the anagram needs its two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaolbird is a habitual prisoner, someone who ought to be locked in prison, speaking of themself.

clue.text: Practice head-rhyme, say, with everybody going for repeat

indicators.note: going means departing, so the word for everyone leaves the longer word

parts.note: to alliterate is to use head-rhyme, words starting with the same sound
all means everybody

explanation.surface: Rehearse a tongue-twister until everyone can say it again.
explanation.walkthrough: Head-rhyme is another name for alliteration; remove ALL from the start.
explanation.definitionFit: To iterate is to repeat, say or do something again, as in reiterate.

clue.text: Troparion about parent who's close?

parts.note: ca. is circa, about
this refers to the one close at hand, as against that
ma is mother

explanation.surface: A hymn about a mother who is near by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This ma' is the close one, as opposed to 'that ma' over there.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathisma is a type of troparion, a short hymn in Orthodox worship during which the congregation may sit.

clue.text: This African language we hear in railway junction

indicators.note: what we hear is a word's sound, not its spelling

parts.note: Crewe in Cheshire is the famous English railway junction town

explanation.surface: A language from Africa is overheard at a train interchange.
explanation.definitionFit: Kroo, or Kru, is a language spoken by the Kru people of Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire in West Africa.

clue.text: Yard accepted conclusion previously acknowledged

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the unit abbreviation takes the shortened word inside

parts.note: yd is the abbreviation for yard
con. is a dictionary abbreviation for conclusion

explanation.surface: A yard took on the final verdict, admitted long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: Y(CON)D. 'Previously' marks an archaic word: ycond is Spenser's form of conned.
explanation.definitionFit: Ycond is an old past participle of con, to know or learn, so it means learnt or acknowledged in earlier English.

clue.text: Pilot is stumped continually being contracted

indicators.note: a contracted word is shortened, here with a letter replaced by an apostrophe

parts.note: st is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for stumped
ever means always, continually

explanation.surface: A pilot is baffled because he keeps getting cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: Ever contracts to the poetic e'er. Stumped is a way a batsman is out in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: To pilot a vessel is to steer it, directing its course.

clue.text: Predator in the main features in "An Inspector Calls"

indicators.note: something that features in a title is a part of it, so the letters lie inside the play's name

parts.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A predator plays a part in J.B. Priestley's famous drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The main is an old word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The orca, or killer whale, is the top predator of the ocean.

clue.text: No more chop chop, poppycock

parts.note: clap is an obsolete word for a chop or blow; 'no more' marks it as old
chops and trap are both slang for the mouth

explanation.surface: Stop hurrying everyone along, that's nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chop chop' looks like 'hurry up'; the two chops are clued separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Claptrap and poppycock are both informal synonyms for nonsense.

clue.text: Peer to give special edge to exquisite huntswoman?

definitions.meaning: a dialect verb: to peep or peer
a rider in a scarlet hunting coat; the question mark marks a woman in one

explanation.surface: A lord sharpens up an elegant woman who rides to hounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Four meanings: peep, cut a zigzag edge, an old sense of exquisite, and one wearing hunting pink, the red coat of the fox hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Pink covers each sense: a dialect verb to peep, the verb for scalloping cloth, an archaic word for finest, and a fox-hunter in red.

clue.text: Shop dished out soups favoured by Asians

indicators.note: dishing out food scatters it around, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A store hands out bowls of broth popular in East Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: Pho is a Vietnamese noodle soup, so phos are servings of the soup popular across South-East Asia.

clue.text: Our town represented as a dead cliché, for example

definitions.text: as a dead cliché, for example

indicators.note: something represented is depicted afresh, so the letters are presented in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Our home town is portrayed as a lifeless stereotype.
explanation.definitionFit: A cliché is a phrase so overused it is stale, which is exactly what worn out describes.

clue.text: Black stuff left in barbie box

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
a barbie is a barbecue, which leaves ash behind

explanation.surface: Charred remains lie in a barbecue's container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a container noun; it is the verb to punch.
explanation.definitionFit: To box someone is to hit them with the fist, and to bash is likewise to strike hard.

clue.text: Unusual ancestor so far wonderfully decent about note

parts.note: 'so far' and 'as far' mean the same, so so = as

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters surround the musical symbol
doing something wonderfully means in a remarkable new way, so the letters of the respectable word are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
N is an abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: A strange forebear, so far, has been remarkably respectable about money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' qualifies the definition: ascendent is a rarer spelling of ascendant, which as a noun means an ancestor.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascendant is a forebear in the direct line of descent, and ascendent is a less common spelling.

clue.text: One intake of undergrads ultimately pay attention

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word
to give ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: New students should, in the end, listen carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pay attention' looks like one phrase but is split.
explanation.definitionFit: A university year is the cohort of students who started together, a single annual intake.

clue.text: Deserted rescue vessel west of promontory poses a mystery

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for deserted
Noah's ark rescued the animals from the flood
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: An abandoned lifeboat beside a headland is a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across answer 'west of' simply means placed before.
explanation.definitionFit: Darkness can mean obscurity or something hidden from understanding, hence a mystery.
